11.ſthe ſtoneI Iacob traueling into a ſtrange countrie went in ſuch
poore ſtate, the better to hide his de parture from Eſau, who otherwiſe might
haue killed him by the way. It was alſo thus diſpoſed by God, that Iacobs
faith and confidence might, to his greatter merite, be exerciſed : and that
Gods prouidence might more manifeſtly appeare, as it did in his returne after
twentie yeares, when with moſt gratſul mind he recounted Gods benefites
ſaying (Gen. 32 ) VVith my ſtaffe I paſſed ouer this Iordan, and now with
two ttoupes I do returne.

18. Erecledit, pevvring eyle I To etect a ſtone, and powre oyle vpon it,
was nowiſe ſuperſticious in Iacob Neither did he lerne it of Idolaters : for
he abhorred and deteſted al idolatrical obſeruances But as S Iuſtinus Martvr
S. Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Euſebius and others teſt: ſie, idolo atrical
ſuperſtition did rather imitate true religious ceremonies. For the diuel al-
wayes affecting that honour, which he ſeeth done to God, perſwaded thoſe
whom he ſeduced, and blinded with errors, to ſerue him in ſuch maner of
external rites, as God was ſerued, that therby he mighteither haue like
worſhip with God, as it happened among Painim Idolaters : or els depriue
God of this kind of honour, as now we ſer Proteſtants reiect and pul downe
conſecrated Altares, pretending them to be ſuperſticious. VVherin they ſhew
moſt groſſe ignotance, if in dede they ſo iudge of ig norance, and not of mere
malice. For who is ſo ſimple, but he may ſee, that the chieſe difference betwen
Religion and Superſtition in external things, conſiſteth in the perſons to
whom they are done, & in the intetion of the doers, & by the ſame diftercnee
of perſons ciuil honour is alſo diſtinguiſhed, from hoth religious and ſuper-
ſticious. As he that knceletl to God, religiouſly honoreth God. kneeling to
the ſunne, moone, or other falfe Gods, ſuperſticicuſlv honoreth the diuel, &
the perſons, & kneeling to the Ring, ciuilly honoreth the king, Iacob without doubt did al
